Topic: When a prince has won his state by the arms of another, how long can he afford to leave those arms unpaid before they become the instrument of his ruin?
Austen — Judgement:
You ask how long a prince may keep his borrowed swords waiting for their wages. I would ask how long any man may keep a creditor who knows his own worth.

In my experience, no one forgives a debt so readily as the debtor, or remembers it so exactly as the creditor. The unpaid soldier is a Wickham with a sword, and his good manners last only as long as his credit. Gratitude is a sentiment of the drawing-room and never a security. What binds men is a motive, and an unpaid motive soon finds another master. The prince flatters himself that arms which conquered for him will rest content with the honour of it, but honour has never settled a tradesman's bill.

He cannot afford a single season, for the day his borrowed arms perceive that they are the true owners of his state, they will begin to behave accordingly.

*Gratitude is the courtesy of the satisfied; the unpaid keep only accounts.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
Not a day longer than the covenant allows, and the covenant is the first morning after victory. Hired swords are men in a state of nature, each ruled by fear of death and appetite for gain, and a prince who owes them wages has made himself their debtor, not their sovereign. Words are but wind: no promise of future payment binds a soldier who holds the sword and sees the treasury. Machiavelli rightly warns that borrowed arms are dangerous, but the deeper cause is that without a common power to keep them in awe, the unpaid will take by force what is denied by contract. Arrears are no mere debt; they are the war of every man against every man, reopened inside the palace walls.

A prince who cannot pay his borrowed arms on the day of victory has already lost his state, for he has armed his creditors against himself.

*Whoever commands a sword he has not paid for commands nothing but the hour of his own betrayal.*
Sun Tzu — Judgement:
Borrowed arms are a debt whose interest is paid in your own sovereignty, and the question is how long before the creditor collects.

Auxiliary troops are, as I wrote, a double danger: they have no master but their pay, and no loyalty but their appetite. A prince who leaves them unpaid has not saved coin; he has taught his strongest men that the throne is cheaper to seize than to serve. What is really at stake is not money but whose hand holds the sword when the accounts fall due. The wise ruler never rests his state on what he cannot command, and he never lets those who can command it feel neglected.

Not one season. Settle what is owed before the army counts its own strength, and in the same breath replace borrowed arms with your own, for an unpaid ally is already a rival who has not yet decided when to strike.

*The army you cannot pay is an army you have already lost, and the one you cannot command is merely waiting for its price.*
